A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Kimi-Dev study. Their text, tables, figures, equations and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original Kimi-Dev benchmark results, training ablations, skill-transfer experiments and appendix case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds end-to-end SWE-Agent RL experiments and a comparative trajectory case study.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 adds end-to-end policy-gradient SWE-Agent adaptation after minimal SFT, extending v1's SFT-only downstream adaptation. This is a limited procedural extension; the architecture and core BugFixer/TestWriter/self-play pipeline remain. The revised optimizer description does not establish that the original model was retrained.

E1.justification: Training sources and evaluated task coverage are retained, including SWE-bench Verified, Live and Multilingual. The new agentic RL experiments reuse SWE-Gym and SWE-bench-extra; the added Matplotlib case remains within existing software issue-resolution coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain the same comparison methods, and existing ablations retain their comparators. The new RL study reuses the MT, SFT and RL priors under a different adaptation protocol rather than introducing another external baseline.

E3.justification: v3 adds a substantially different adaptation experiment: one SFT step using 2^21 tokens, followed by end-to-end RL with pass@8 prompt filtering, batch size 256 and no KL or entropy regularization. It reports 260 retained problems for MT versus 2,062 for the SFT/RL priors, with the latter trained for 300 steps. Existing experimental protocols are retained.

E4.justification: New Section 4.2 experiments test whether prior quality persists under end-to-end RL with minimal expert imitation, substantially extending the previous SFT-based analysis. New Appendix G.3 compares heavy-SFT and light-SFT-plus-RL trajectories on matplotlib-13989. Earlier ablations, failure cases and generalization analyses remain.

E5.justification: New Figure 7 reports pass@1 averaged over five runs with min–max bands. This adds variability reporting for the new experiment; it does not establish additional runs for existing experiments or five independent training seeds.

E6.justification: Figure 7 adds pass@1, pass@3 and pass@5 learning curves showing a modest RL-prior advantage over the SFT prior. New text reports MT performance falling below 2% after ten RL steps, and Appendix G.3 adds qualitative trajectory findings. Existing scores, including 60.4% and 48.6% in Tables 1–2, are unchanged; the additions are results under new training conditions.

T1.justification: v3 removes v1 Appendix C.1, including Equation 2's explicit RL objective, mathematical definitions and reference-policy penalty explanation. The replacement REINFORCE description supplies no equivalent formal objective. The self-play scoring equation remains unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central claims: Agentless training produces transferable skill priors, achieves 60.4% workflow performance and enables 48.6% SWE-Agent performance through SFT. The shortened conclusion preserves these contributions; the new experiments provide additional support.

C2.justification: v3 interprets minimally supervised agentic RL as evidence beyond expert imitation and suggests insufficient usable training problems explain MT's collapse. Appendix G.3 attributes more exploratory, reasoning-intensive trajectories to RL versus heavy SFT. Existing TestWriter coverage and reflection-measurement limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents filtering, training budgets, batch size and regularization choices for the new agentic RL experiments, while removing the explicit original RL objective. Existing implementation descriptions, prompts and access information remain. The 1,200-problem initial curriculum and 500-problem additions were already documented in v1 Appendix C.2.

R1.justification: v3 adds Williams (1992) to ground the REINFORCE description and Gudibande et al. (2024) to motivate testing beyond imitation. It removes Nachum et al. (2017) and the conclusion's alignment/safety future-work citations. The broader research positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Local revisions simplify the RL and main-results explanations, shorten the conclusion, remove Appendix C.1 and insert Appendix G.3. The erroneous statement that the RL prior 'is outperformed' becomes 'outperforms,' matching the retained Figure 5. The overall narrative and organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v3 adds the three-panel Figure 7 and two trajectory listings, compresses Table 1, and resizes or relocates several existing figures. Original plotted content is retained, including the generalization plots renumbered as Figures 11–12. These are localized presentation changes rather than a comprehensive redesign.

improvement.justification: The new end-to-end RL comparison and Appendix G.3 provide useful evidence that skill priors support adaptation beyond extensive expert imitation, and the Figure 5 prose contradiction is corrected. The gain is limited by the modest prior-performance difference and single selected qualitative case. Removing the explicit RL objective also reduces mathematical reproducibility, but the added validation yields a net improvement.
